strengths: The core observation is clean and interesting: modeling a categorical distribution as a hierarchical sequence of binary decisions (with an appropriate activation) yields a diagonal Fisher Information Matrix, and the paper proves this rigorously (Theorem 4.2, Appendices B-C), including a useful corollary (4.3) showing the 'natural activation' ν(x) makes each diagonal entry independent of the local score.
The proposed parameterization is a simple, drop-in replacement for softmax that is compatible with standard estimators (REINFORCE, Gumbel-Softmax, PPO), which makes the contribution easy to adopt.

Evaluation spans three genuinely different domains (graph structure learning with score-function gradients, categorical VAEs with Gumbel-Softmax, and PPO on Atari), which is a thoughtful design for testing generality across gradient estimator types.

The GSL experiment is well designed around entropy of the true latent distribution (Table 1) and includes a proper ground-truth/optimal-value reference; the latent-calibration metric (MAE on θ) shows a clear, meaningful improvement for the natural activation.
Reproducibility is treated seriously: full proofs, detailed experimental appendices (D-F), hyperparameter search procedures for RL, and an explicit LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Missing engagement with closely related prior work. The hierarchical binary-split construction is essentially the classical stick-breaking representation of a simplex (Sethuraman, 1994) and is closely related to hierarchical softmax (Morin & Bengio, 2005) and tree-structured parameterizations; none of these are cited or compared. This also undercuts the claim of being 'the first work to use information geometry to study the softmax parameterization', which is overclaimed.

The link between a diagonal FIM and better practical training is weakly established. Standard optimizers (SGD, Adam) do not precondition by the FIM, and for a single categorical variable the softmax FIM is only K×K and trivially invertible, so the computational arguments about natural-gradient bottlenecks do not really apply here. The theoretical result is correct but the causal story for the empirical gains is more of a plausibility argument than a demonstration; no direct diagnostic (e.g., conditioning of the parameter space, update path analysis) connects theory to experiments.

The main theoretical claim (hierarchical vs. softmax) is not actually tested in the GSL experiment: with bivariate variables, softmax and sigmoid parameterizations are equivalent, so Section 5.1 only compares activation functions, not the central parameterization choice.

Class-ordering dependence is unaddressed. The hierarchical construction imposes an arbitrary ordering/binary coding of classes, and performance may depend on this permutation; the paper neither analyzes this nor discusses how to choose the tree structure.

Practical coverage is narrower than the abstract implies: K is restricted to powers of two (H = log2 K), so common cases like K = 10 (MNIST digits, vocabulary tokens) are not handled by the presented construction; the VAE experiments use only K ∈ {8, 16, 32} on MNIST, and RL uses only two Atari games where the reported gains (406±34 vs 398±25 on Breakout) are within overlapping error bars.

Improvement magnitudes are modest in the strongest-known baselines' territory (roughly 1-2 nats of NLL on MNIST VAE), and while consistent, the paper provides limited statistical testing (e.g., no paired tests in Tables 3-4) to support the 'consistently higher test performance' claim.

Proposition 4.1 is essentially a textbook result (the categorical FIM under softmax), and the FIM's rank deficiency due to softmax overparameterization — which is arguably the more relevant information-geometric issue — is mentioned only in passing as 'overparameterized' without connecting it to the analysis.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the mathematical development is clean: the proofs that the softmax FIM is dense (Prop. 4.1) and that the hierarchical (catnat) parameterization yields a diagonal FIM (Thm. 4.2, Cor. 4.3) are correct and easy to follow.

The proposed change is genuinely simple and practical: it is a drop-in replacement for softmax, is orthogonal to gradient-estimation techniques, and the paper evaluates it in three different domains (GSL, categorical VAEs, RL) rather than a single benchmark.

Reproducibility is addressed seriously: the method is fully specified, experimental setups build on public codebases, and hyperparameter search procedures are documented (Appendices D–F), including an honest account of how learning rates were tuned per parameterization.

The experiments include some consistently positive results, notably the categorical VAE results (Table 3), where both catnat variants improve over softmax across all (N, K) settings, and the improved recovery of the true latent parameters (MAE on θ) in the GSL experiments.
weaknesses: Limited originality: factorizing a categorical distribution as a sequence of binary decisions (tree-structured / hierarchical softmax-style parameterizations, stick-breaking, Dirichlet-tree distributions) is well established in statistics and machine learning, and the fact that such parameterizations decouple the parameters (yielding a diagonal FIM) is essentially known. The claim that this is 'the first work to use information geometry to study the softmax parameterization' is overstated.

The central mechanistic claim — that a diagonal FIM leads to better gradient descent in practice — is not actually established. The paper shows the softmax FIM is dense and the catnat FIM is diagonal, but provides no analysis or direct empirical evidence linking this geometric property to improved optimization of the full end-to-end loss (the FIMs are for the local categorical parameterization, while the experiments optimize a global non-convex objective through deep networks). This is a heuristic motivation presented as if it were a supported explanation.

The RL evidence is weak: only two Atari environments, with Seaquest results (1875±312 vs 2164±533) well within one standard deviation and Breakout showing a negligible difference. The text's claim of a 'consistent performance advantage despite this variance' is not supported by the reported statistics, and no significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper.

The VAE gains are modest (roughly 1–3 nats of NLL) and the paper itself concedes that the sigmoid and natural catnat variants are 'statistically equivalent on average'. Moreover, the interplay between catnat and the Gumbel-Softmax trick is unclear: sampling under a hierarchical parameterization is not the Gumbel-Softmax construction, and the paper does not explain how reparameterization and gradient flow are actually handled for catnat, which is central to interpreting Table 3.

The hierarchical parameterization imposes an arbitrary binary tree structure on the K categories, introducing label-order dependence that softmax does not have; this potential drawback, and the handling of non-power-of-two K, are not discussed.

The 'natural activation' function is an ad hoc sinusoidal construction whose benefit over a plain sigmoid is marginal in most experiments; the one domain with the largest claimed gains (GSL) is fully synthetic and uses depth-one hierarchies (i.e., bivariate Bernoulli), so it does not exercise the main contribution (deep hierarchies) at all.

Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence ('yields models characterized by consistently higher test performance', 'offers a better alternative to the softmax function'), while the reported margins are frequently within error bars.

No comparison against other structured parameterizations (e.g., stick-breaking variants, learned/permuted trees, hierarchical softmax with different tree shapes), which is necessary to isolate whether the gains come from the diagonal-FIM property specifically or merely from a different (constrained) parameterization family.

strengths: The paper takes a genuinely interesting and complementary angle on the well-studied problem of learning with latent categorical variables: rather than improving gradient estimators, it changes the parameterization of the categorical distribution itself, motivated by information geometry.

The theoretical results (Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3) are clearly stated, and the proofs in Appendices A–C are correct and self-contained; the hierarchical binary-decision construction (catnat) does yield a diagonal FIM, and the natural activation function cleanly removes the score-dependence of the diagonal entries.

The method is simple, essentially a drop-in replacement for softmax, and the paper demonstrates breadth by evaluating across three quite different domains (GSL, categorical VAEs, RL/PPO), with reproducibility supported by detailed appendices and public codebases.

The paper is generally well-written, and the limitations are acknowledged fairly honestly (e.g., hyperparameter search constraints in RL, statistical equivalence of the two catnat variants in the VAE experiments).
weaknesses: Missing engagement with closely related prior work weakens the originality claim. Tree/chain-structured factorizations of categorical distributions (e.g., hierarchical softmax, stick-breaking/telescoping parameterizations, sequential binary decompositions) are well known, and diagonality of the FIM for such product-form tree factorizations is essentially a standard consequence of the chain-rule structure. The claim that this is 'the first work to use information geometry to study the softmax parameterization' needs to be substantiated against this literature, which is not cited.

The central causal claim — that a diagonal FIM improves *vanilla* gradient descent — is not directly validated. All experiments use Adam, which already performs diagonal per-parameter preconditioning, so the information-geometric motivation and the observed gains may be decoupled: improvements could instead stem from the different inductive bias of the hierarchical factorization (class ordering, depth-wise conditioning). There are no experiments with plain SGD or an explicit natural-gradient baseline that would isolate the geometric effect.

The diagonal entries G_ν(s)_ii still depend on P(a_i) (the ancestor probabilities), so the manifold is not actually flattened to constant curvature; the 'natural' framing is therefore only partial, and the paper does not analyze how the remaining ancestor-dependent term affects optimization.

Sensitivity to the assignment of classes to tree leaves (the binary ordering) is a crucial design choice for catnat but is never discussed or ablated. Similarly, the construction assumes K = 2^H (all main experiments use K ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32}), yet the RL experiments use Atari action spaces that are not powers of two; how catnat handles general K is unspecified.

Empirical effect sizes are modest and statistical rigor is thin. In the GSL experiment improvements are on the order of 0.02–0.03 in the ES loss; VAE gains are ~1–2 nats and the two catnat variants are admittedly 'statistically equivalent on average'; the RL evaluation covers only two Atari environments with overlapping error bars (Breakout: 398±25 vs 406±34), and no significance tests are reported anywhere.

The integration of catnat with the Gumbel-Softmax trick in the VAE experiments is not precisely specified (Gumbel-max sampling operates on logits of a categorical; it is unclear how discrete samples and the straight-through relaxation are obtained from the hierarchical sigmoid/sin activations), which is important for reproducibility of the strongest empirical table.

Some overclaiming in framing: the abstract and conclusions suggest catnat 'offers a better alternative to the softmax function' broadly, but the evidence supports only modest, setting-dependent improvements, and the paper's own conclusions concede the experiments were not designed for state-of-the-art comparisons.

strengths: Clean and correct core theoretical result: Proposition 4.1 shows the softmax FIM is dense, and Theorem 4.2 (with complete proofs in Appendices B-D) shows the hierarchical binary-split parameterization induces a diagonal FIM at the score level; the 'natural activation' that additionally makes the diagonal entries constant (Corollary 4.3) is a neat design choice with no extra tuned hyperparameters.

The paper is unusually candid about the scope of its theory: Section 4.2.3 explicitly derives the pulled-back FIM w.r.t. network parameters (Eqs. 14-15) and clarifies that only cross-score coupling is removed, not a globally diagonal FIM. This honest scoping is a positive.

Empirical evaluation is broad (graph structure learning, categorical VAEs on MNIST/Binary MNIST across N and K, PPO on Atari), uses statistical testing (Welch's t-test), includes an SGD-vs-Adam ablation (Appendix G), an independent VAE codebase check (Appendix H), and baselines beyond softmax (sparsemax, catnat-with-sigmoid), which lets the reader separate the hierarchy effect from the activation effect.

The method is simple, drop-in compatible with standard estimators (REINFORCE, Gumbel-Softmax, PPO), and orthogonal to variance-reduction techniques, making the contribution easy for others to build on.
weaknesses: Limited originality: parameterizing a categorical as a tree/sequence of Bernoulli decisions is well established (hierarchical softmax, Morin & Bengio 2005; Mnih & Hinton 2008), and the diagonal-FIM property of conditionally independent binary splits is a fairly direct consequence of that factorization. The claim of being 'the first work to use information geometry to study the softmax and replace it' is overstated given this literature, which the paper itself acknowledges the hierarchical classifiers are special cases of.

The causal link between the theory and the empirical gains is weak. Vanilla gradient descent and Adam do not use the FIM; a diagonal score-level FIM helps only via the heuristic argument in Appendix A (that Adam approximates the diagonal rescaling). The paper provides no direct evidence (e.g., gradient-conditioning measurements, or comparison against an explicit diagonal natural-gradient preconditioner) that the diagonal FIM is the mechanism, rather than, e.g., gradient bounding from the saturating activation or an implicit entropy effect. Figure 1, a 2-D slice of a 3-parameter landscape, is anecdotal support.

The natural activation ν saturates to 0/1 outside |s_i - C| < A/2, making the FIM exactly zero there (Corollary 4.3). This reintroduces the vanishing-gradient / dead-unit problem the paper criticizes softmax for, and no analysis or mitigation (e.g., gradients when all scores saturate) is given.

Class-ordering sensitivity is not analyzed. Catnat imposes an arbitrary binary hierarchy on classes; performance may depend on the permutation of labels/actions, which is critical for RL action spaces and classification. For non-power-of-2 K (e.g., Seaquest has 6 actions), the construction with H = log2(K) bits is not specified.

Empirical margins are modest in places: VAE NLL improvements over softmax are ~1-2 nats, RL results cover only two Atari environments with substantial variance (Breakout 398±25 vs 406±34 is marginal), and the Appendix H ELBO results for catnat ν show very large variance at N=10 (-122.7±33.4), hinting at instability not discussed.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code-availability URLs in the abstract and Section 1 are blank ('available at and'), and several experimental details (K selection, how non-power-of-2 K is handled in RL, exact VAE hyperparameters for Table 3) are incomplete or absent.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the information-geometric framing is pedagogically useful: the derivation of the softmax FIM (Prop 4.1) and the diagonal-FIM result for the hierarchical binary-split parameterization (Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3) are correct, with full proofs in the appendix.
The proposed catnat parameterization is genuinely simple to implement and drop-in compatible with existing codebases, which increases its practical appeal.

The empirical evaluation is broader than typical for a parameterization paper, spanning three domains (synthetic graph structure learning, categorical VAEs on MNIST/Binary MNIST, and PPO on Atari), with Welch's t-tests, multiple seeds, and SGD-vs-Adam robustness checks plus a second independent VAE codebase.

The authors are commendably honest about the scope of the theory: Section 4.2.3 explicitly states that the diagonal FIM holds only in score space, not w.r.t. network parameters, and the conclusions acknowledge the experiments were not designed for state-of-the-art claims.
weaknesses: Limited originality. The core construction is essentially a hierarchical binary factorization of a categorical distribution — closely related to hierarchical softmax (Morin & Bengio, 2005; Mnih & Hinton, 2008), which the authors cite but do not convincingly differentiate beyond the activation choice. That a chain of independent Bernoulli decisions yields a diagonal FIM is a fairly direct consequence of the factorized likelihood, and the softmax FIM formula itself is well known. The claim of being 'the first work to use information geometry to study the softmax parameterization' is overstated given the substantial natural-gradient literature.

The central claim — that a diagonal score-space FIM yields better gradient-descent optimization — is only loosely connected to the evidence. The paper itself concedes the pulled-back FIM w.r.t. θ is dense (Eq. 15), and the link to why this helps Adam/PPO is heuristic (Appendix A hand-waves that Adam 'approximates' coordinate-wise rescaling). Figure 1 is a single two-dimensional slice of a toy landscape and offers weak support.

A critical confound is not addressed: unlike softmax, catnat imposes a fixed, arbitrary binary ordering of categories, so the parameterization is not permutation-symmetric. No ablation over category permutations or tree structures is provided, so it is impossible to tell whether reported gains come from the FIM properties or from incidental label-to-leaf assignments.

Empirical support is narrow and modest. RL uses only two Atari games with small, high-variance gains (Breakout: 398±25 vs 406±34 is within noise); the VAE results are confined to MNIST variants; the GSL setting is purely synthetic. The motivated domains where softmax dominates in practice (e.g., language modeling) are absent. Table 6 shows catnat ν with very large instability (−122.7 ± 33.4), which the text does not discuss.

Hyperparameter treatment raises fairness concerns: in the GSL experiments the refined learning-rate grids differ between parameterizations (sigmoid vs. natural use different, non-overlapping grids), and the natural activation requires roughly half the learning rate, suggesting sensitivity of the method rather than robust improvement.

The natural activation function ν has exactly-zero gradients outside the interval |s−C| < A/2, meaning nodes can die irreversibly during training; this known pathology of hard-saturated activations is neither discussed nor empirically probed (e.g., dead-node statistics).
Reproducibility is weakened by missing/cut-off code links in the manuscript text ('available at and'), and several key details (e.g., how catnat handles K not a power of two) are not specified.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 (with the proofs in Appendices B–D) are correct and carefully derived, and the derivation in Section 4.2.3 honestly clarifies that the diagonal FIM is local to the score space rather than the network parameters — a nuance many papers of this type would omit.

The proposed approach is simple, drop-in, and compatible with existing gradient estimators (REINFORCE, Gumbel-Softmax) and optimizers; the authors convincingly argue orthogonality to the existing variance-reduction literature.

Empirical evaluation spans three distinct domains (GSL, categorical VAEs, RL), includes ablations (SGD vs Adam, a second VAE codebase), statistical testing (Welch's t-test), and reasonable hyperparameter search procedures, showing consistent gains for catnat over softmax and sparsemax.

The information-geometric motivation is clearly presented, and the paper honestly separates what is proven (diagonal score-space FIM) from what is empirically observed (better optimization), rather than overclaiming.
Implementations in PyTorch and JAX are released, and experimental details in the appendices are thorough, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core conceptual novelty is limited: tree-structured/hierarchical decompositions of categorical distributions are well established (Morin & Bengio 2005; Mnih & Hinton 2008), and the diagonal-FIM property follows almost directly from the conditional-independence structure of the tree. The paper's contribution is mainly a re-framing via information geometry plus the 'natural activation' ν, which is a modest delta.

The link between a diagonal local FIM and better downstream optimization is heuristic. Figure 1 shows only a 2-D slice of a 3-parameter toy problem; the theory says nothing about the curvature of the actual loss landscapes used in the experiments, and the downstream objectives (ELBO, PPO surrogate, Energy Score) are not log-likelihoods of the categorical model, so the FIM argument only loosely applies.

Important practical limitations are not discussed. (i) The natural activation ν is piecewise constant outside [C−A/2, C+A/2], introducing hard saturation and potential dead nodes — precisely the vanishing-gradient pathology the paper criticizes in softmax; this interacts badly with the annealing/score-saturation regimes common in RL and deep training and is never analyzed. (ii) The construction requires H = log2(K) levels, apparently restricting K to powers of two (all experiments use K ∈ {8,16,32}); handling arbitrary K is not addressed. (iii) The parameterization is tied to a fixed binary index ordering, so it is not permutation-invariant in the labels, unlike softmax; sensitivity to class ordering could affect results and should be examined.

The sparsemax baseline is a weak/odd comparator — it is motivated by sparsity, not by optimization geometry — and no comparison against a tuned hierarchical softmax or a temperature-controlled softmax is provided.

The RL evidence is thin: only two Atari environments, with Breakout showing near-overlapping statistics (398±25 vs 406±34), and Table 6 reveals substantial instability for catnat ν at small N (−122.7±33.4 ELBO), which is not analyzed or discussed.

Hyperparameter search procedures differ across parameterizations (e.g., different refined learning-rate grids for sigmoid vs natural activation in Appendix E.2), which, while arguably fair, introduces a possible source of tuning asymmetry that the paper does not discuss.
